strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/6c82d32a1aaf4ec9aea9a6176a446339/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents an interesting and reasonably original formulation of symmetry discovery as flow matching along Lie-group orbits. Using exponential-map updates keeps generated trajectories compatible with the chosen group action, and treating continuous and finite target structures in one framework is appealing.

The experiments cover several distinct settings—SO(2), GL(2,R)+, GL(2,C), and SO(3) hypotheses; cyclic, dihedral, polyhedral, and continuous targets—and include a multi-object test rather than only a single canonical object.

The identification of late convergence for symmetrically arranged modes is potentially useful. The power time-sampling heuristic produces a visually substantial improvement for the octahedral example without changing the network.

The paper is generally readable and visually well organized. It candidly reports important failures, including the inability to recover the icosahedral group, and appropriately acknowledges the restriction to simple noise-free point clouds and prescribed low-dimensional hypothesis groups.
No material research-ethics concerns are apparent, and the paper provides a transparent statement of LLM assistance.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is insufficiently justified. Training learns a data-conditioned transport from g x to the data distribution; it does not directly learn a single, data-independent distribution supported on the global stabilizer H. Algorithm 3 returns transformations that depend on the sampled object x, but the paper neither proves that these transformations lie in the distribution stabilizer nor tests closure, inverses, composition, or invariance q(hx)=q(x) on held-out data. Good endpoint alignment alone is not sufficient evidence of group discovery.

The posterior analysis underlying the claimed “last-minute mode convergence” appears technically invalid. In Algorithm 4, p(x_t|x_1) is evaluated by integrating the divergence of the learned marginal velocity field from an x_0 obtained by inverting a conditional linear interpolant. That marginal flow does not provide the conditional-path likelihood for a specified x_1, and its simulated trajectory need not pass through the queried x_t. Periodicity of SO(2) and wrapping at the cut are also absent. Consequently, the entropy plots do not reliably establish the stated posterior behavior.

Several mathematical statements need correction or qualification. Connectedness does not ensure a globally well-defined, unique logarithm on compact groups such as SO(2) or SO(3); branch and cut-locus choices matter. Sampling Lie-algebra coefficients and exponentiating also does not cover a non-surjective exponential map. Moreover, the main text says noncompact priors use Gaussian coefficients, whereas Appendix B specifies bounded uniform coefficients for GL(2), and the Riemannian norm in Eq. 5 is replaced by an unexplained Euclidean squared loss in Algorithm 1.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the paper's broad claims: all principal tasks are constructed, noise-free point-cloud orbits with known hypothesis groups and known transformations. There are no approximate/noisy or realistic datasets, no downstream utility experiment, and no comparison to the closest cited generative/canonicalization approach. A simple nearest-orbit or canonicalization baseline is also missing.

LieGAN is the only quantitative baseline, yet it is designed around exponentiated Lie generators and is structurally poorly matched to finite disconnected subgroups. Varying its generator count does not establish a fair or comprehensive comparison. There are no multiple-seed results, uncertainty estimates, capacity-matched controls, or ablations of the power exponent, timestep weighting, solver steps, complex parameterization, and network capacity.

The quantitative protocol is underspecified. The ground metric used for Wasserstein-1 on matrices/group elements, treatment of SO(3) geometry, empirical target weights, canonicalization, and whether Table 2's octahedral result uses the power schedule are not stated clearly. The latter is particularly confusing because the uniform-time model is reported to fail on Oct while Table 2 reports a very low distance.

The time-sampling proposal changes the weighting of the regression objective but not its population conditional-mean solution at each time. Its benefit therefore appears to concern finite-capacity optimization, yet this explanation is not examined experimentally. Calling it a novel interpolation scheme is also inaccurate because the interpolation path is unchanged.

The Gaussian-angle experiment is described as retaining SO(2) symmetry, but a nonuniform Gaussian distribution over rotation angles is not invariant under arbitrary SO(2) actions and therefore does not satisfy the paper's own definition q(hx)=q(x). It demonstrates recovery of a transformation distribution, not symmetry discovery.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the manuscript omits layer widths, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training duration, dataset sizes/splits, normalization, random seeds, Lie-algebra basis scaling, matrix-log implementation, numerical tolerances, and full baseline tuning. No code or configuration artifact is provided despite reliance on complex-valued networks and delicate logarithm/exponential computations.

strengths: Originality: The paper offers an interesting synthesis of flow matching on Lie groups and symmetry discovery, with a unified attempt to represent continuous and finite transformation distributions.

Soundness: The orbit-constrained interpolation and Lie-algebra parameterization are intuitively motivated, and several synthetic experiments show convincing recovery of simple groups such as C4, the tetrahedral group, and axial SO(2).

Analysis: Identifying the late concentration of flow trajectories is potentially useful. The paper does not conceal failures on the octahedral and icosahedral groups, and it tests a simple power time-sampling heuristic that improves the octahedral result.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally organized and visually clear, with trajectory plots, generated transformations, algorithms, and an appendix containing additional experiments.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section candidly acknowledges the restriction to clean synthetic point clouds, dependence on a prescribed hypothesis group, poor scaling to complex symmetries, and unresolved real-world applicability. LLM use is disclosed, and the work raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of discovering a stabilizer subgroup is stronger than what is established. The method learns an aggregate, data-conditioned distribution of transformations observed under a user-specified hypothesis group, but it neither enforces nor verifies closure, inverses, or identity. Thus, an arbitrary multimodal transformation distribution could be reported as a discovered group.

Soundness: The derivation relies on the orbit map having a trivial stabilizer so that a data-space tangent has a unique Lie-algebra coordinate. This is stated only in Appendix A, while the experiments deliberately use canonical objects without self-symmetries. Many intended symmetry-discovery settings have nontrivial stabilizers, where the regression target is ambiguous; the paper neither resolves nor experimentally studies this central case.

Soundness: The posterior computation supporting the claimed 'last-minute mode convergence' appears invalid. Algorithm 4 inverts the conditional linear interpolant for each candidate endpoint but then evolves that point using the learned marginal velocity field. Such a trajectory is not the endpoint-conditioned interpolation and therefore does not provide p(x_t | x_1). The calculation also substitutes an arbitrary Gaussian with sigma 0.1 near t=1 and does not handle the circular topology of SO(2) rigorously. Consequently, the entropy plots do not substantiate the claimed posterior behavior.

Evaluation: All demonstrations use tiny, clean, synthetically generated point clouds with the hypothesis and target groups known during experiment design. There are no noisy or approximate symmetries, real data, high-dimensional groups, or downstream equivariant-learning experiments. Claims concerning practical discovery, sample efficiency, and generalization are therefore unsupported.

Evaluation: LieGAN is the only quantitative baseline and is not evidently suited to representing finite multimodal subgroups, making it a weak comparator. Relevant symmetry-discovery and generative-transformation methods discussed in related work are not evaluated. Even against LieGAN, improvements for GL(2,R)+ to C4 and GL(2,C) to D4 are small and absolute Wasserstein distances remain large.

Evaluation: The quantitative protocol is underspecified. The manuscript does not define the ground cost or computation used for Wasserstein-1 on group elements, provide uncertainty over random seeds, report sample-efficiency or computational cost, or give ablations for the power exponent, integration steps, architecture, complex representation, and inference discretization. Table 2 reports strong octahedral performance without clearly stating that it uses the power schedule, despite Section 5.2 reporting failure with uniform sampling.

Reproducibility: The appendix omits essential information including exact layer widths, dataset sizes and splits, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training duration, initialization, stopping criteria, baseline tuning, and code availability. Descriptions such as a 'simple 3-layer MLP' are insufficient to reproduce the reported results.

Presentation and formal precision: The text incorrectly suggests connectedness ensures a well-defined logarithm for compact groups; global logarithms can be multivalued and have cut loci. It also alternates between left- and right-multiplication conventions, calls x0 both a data-space sample and an element of G, invokes an unspecified Riemannian metric while apparently training with ordinary coefficient MSE, and labels the power time-sampling heuristic a new interpolation scheme even though the interpolation is unchanged.

Significance: The method fails on the icosahedral group even in the highly favorable synthetic setting, requires choosing a containing group in advance, and has no demonstrated mechanism for deciding whether its learned modes constitute a group. These limitations substantially reduce its present usefulness as a general symmetry-discovery method.

Overall: The idea is promising and the candid negative results are valuable, but the unsupported subgroup interpretation, questionable posterior analysis, narrow and weakly controlled evaluation, and inadequate reproducibility are material deficiencies. They outweigh the paper's originality and presentation quality, so acceptance is not justified in its current form.

Significance: A unified mechanism capable of representing both continuous and discrete symmetries would be useful, and the reported successes on C4, D4, tetrahedral, octahedral, and SO(2) targets provide encouraging proof-of-concept evidence.

Soundness: The paper does more than report favorable results: it exposes the failure on the octahedral and icosahedral groups, investigates the learned trajectories, and proposes a simple time-sampling intervention that visibly improves the octahedral case.

Presentation: The high-level motivation, algorithms, trajectory plots, and limitations are generally clear. The paper distinguishes the hypothesis group from the target subgroup and openly limits its empirical claims to simple, noise-free point clouds.

Ethics and limitations: No material ethical concerns are apparent. The authors appropriately disclose LLM assistance and candidly discuss restrictions to prescribed hypothesis groups, low-dimensional settings, and synthetic data.
weaknesses: Soundness: The posterior computation supporting the central “last-minute mode convergence” analysis appears inconsistent. Appendix D inverts the prescribed linear interpolant but then uses the unconditional learned velocity field and its continuity equation to estimate p(x_t|x_1). That procedure yields a marginal-flow density, not the conditional interpolant density required by Bayes' rule. The Gaussian substitution near t=1 is also heuristic. Consequently, Figures 7 and 30 do not yet provide reliable evidence for the claimed posterior-entropy behavior.

Soundness: The mathematical treatment of logarithms and geometry is incomplete. Connectedness does not ensure a globally unique, well-defined logarithm, notably for SO(3); cut-locus and branch choices can change training targets. Equation 5 invokes a left-invariant Riemannian metric, but the implementation appears to use an ordinary coordinate-space squared loss without specifying the basis, metric, or complex-valued norm. The method also requires a trivial sample stabilizer for unique Lie-algebra coordinates, an important restriction not tested experimentally.

Evaluation: All principal experiments use small synthetic, noiseless point clouds generated from known groups. There are no approximate/noisy symmetries, real data, downstream equivariance or sample-efficiency experiments, or scaling studies. Thus the broad usefulness suggested in the introduction remains unverified.

Evaluation: The comparison is limited to LieGAN, despite the paper identifying Allingham et al. as the closest method and discussing multiple discrete-symmetry approaches. There is no simple registration, clustering, or nearest-orbit baseline. The improvements are sometimes modest, and no multiple-seed means, error bars, sensitivity analyses, runtime, or parameter comparisons are reported.

Evaluation clarity: Table 2 reports an excellent octahedral Wasserstein distance even though the uniform-time model is said to fail and resemble the prior. It is unclear whether the table uses the power-schedule model. More generally, the ground cost, normalization, OT estimator, canonicalization procedure, and uncertainty for the Wasserstein metric are not defined, making the headline quantitative results difficult to interpret.

Conceptual scope: Learning transformations that map one observed orbit element to another is not by itself sufficient to establish recovery of the full distribution stabilizer in general, especially with multiple orbits, nontrivial object stabilizers, or approximate symmetries. The nonuniform Gaussian SO(2) experiment further shifts from distributional symmetry—whose stabilizer is generally not SO(2)—to learning “structure-preserving transformations,” blurring the stated problem definition.

Reproducibility: The appendix omits essential hyperparameters and data details, including dataset sizes, exact layer widths, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training duration, initialization, seeds, log/exponential implementations, metric choices, and LieGAN tuning. No code or availability statement is provided. These gaps prevent reliable reproduction and, together with the posterior issue and narrow evaluation, outweigh the paper's promising idea in its current form.

strengths: The formulation of symmetry discovery as learning a distribution over transformations is original and potentially useful, especially because one model can represent both continuous and multimodal discrete transformation sets.

The paper is generally clear and well organized. Algorithms, architectures, priors, and the motivation for the power time schedule are described, and the visualizations make the learned transformation distributions reasonably interpretable.

The experiments cover several hypothesis groups, discrete and continuous targets, two GL(2) priors, incomplete point clouds, and a partially observed setting. On the constructed benchmarks, LieFlow substantially improves over the reported LieGAN results for discrete groups.

The analysis of late mode convergence identifies a genuine practical difficulty of flow matching with discrete targets. The time-sampling ablation provides useful empirical evidence for the proposed mitigation.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges restricted scale, dependence on group parameterization, and the need to extend beyond small point clouds. LLM use is disclosed, and the work raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central identification claim is not established. Training on pairs x0 = g x1 and x1 teaches a conditional denoising or transport map from the group-augmented distribution back to q. It does not imply that each accumulated, input-dependent transformation Mg is a global symmetry satisfying q(hx) = q(x). A transformation may map one particular input to another likely sample without preserving q when applied globally. The manuscript's informal assertion that nonsymmetry directions cancel is not a proof and does not rule out such conditional solutions.

Relatedly, marginalizing the input-dependent transformations and interpreting the support of that marginal as a subgroup is generally unjustified: support need not be closed under composition or inversion, and correlations between a generated transformation and the conditioning object are discarded. No quantitative closure, inverse, or global invariance tests are reported.

The partially observed C4 experiment illustrates this conceptual problem. The distribution supported on rotations {0, 90, 270} degrees is not C4-invariant. Recovering the missing 180-degree relative transformation does not establish that C4 is a symmetry of that data distribution; 180 degrees maps some supported observations to absent ones. Thus the result supports completion of pairwise relative transformations, not the claimed recovery of a true symmetry group.

The empirical evidence is narrowly constructed. Even the ModelNet10 data are artificially generated by applying known target-group transformations to only 100 selected canonical objects, so describing this as real-world symmetry discovery overstates the evaluation. There are no naturally occurring unknown symmetries, downstream benefits, approximate-symmetry evaluations, or high-dimensional/noncompact cases beyond a small GL(2) experiment.

The comparison is insufficient to substantiate state-of-the-art performance. Only LieGAN is evaluated, although the related-work section identifies other symmetry-discovery and transformation-distribution methods. LieGAN is known by the authors' own discussion to require an appropriate multimodal prior for discrete groups, but the comparison appears to use a setup poorly suited to that case. No careful hyperparameter budget or competitive discrete-group baseline is provided.

Results are single point estimates without variation across seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The skewness parameter is selected on the same SO(3)-to-Ico setting used to demonstrate improvement, leaving its robustness and generalization unclear.

Several mathematical qualifications are missing or inaccurate. Connectedness does not provide a globally well-defined logarithm on compact groups; logarithms may be multivalued and discontinuous. The appendix's identification of a data-space tangent vector with a unique Lie-algebra element requires a trivial stabilizer, an assumption that is not guaranteed for ModelNet objects and conflicts with the broader claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper omits code availability, random seeds, dataset sample counts after augmentation, training epochs or stopping rules, inference integration steps for reported tables, full baseline tuning details, and the precise SO(3)/GL(2) ground metric used in Wasserstein evaluation. These omissions make the large reported performance gaps difficult to independently verify.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/39ab51e7527f4c158914bc79026628e9/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents an original and intuitive formulation of symmetry discovery as flow matching over a prescribed Lie-group hypothesis space. It can represent discrete and continuous transformation distributions within one framework.

The controlled experiments cover several target subgroups, including C4, tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral, and SO(2) subgroups. The qualitative visualizations generally agree with the reported Wasserstein results, and the power-schedule ablation identifies a useful empirical optimization effect for larger discrete groups.

The paper is mostly readable, gives explicit training and sampling algorithms, discusses limitations such as scalability and prior parameterization, and discloses its use of LLMs. The work appears low-risk ethically, with no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central identification claim is not established. Conditional flow matching can learn a transport from transformed samples back to the data distribution even when the latter has no group invariance. The paper's explanation that invalid transformations produce directions that “cancel out” is informal and generally insufficient to show that the returned transformations have support exactly equal to a subgroup H. At most, the construction can recover transformations relating observations within the same orbit; additional assumptions are needed for those transformations to be global symmetries of q.

The partial-symmetry experiment exposes this conceptual problem. A distribution supported equally on arrow orientations {0, π/2, 3π/2} is not invariant under C4, yet the method reports C4 because pairwise relative transformations cover the missing element. Thus it recovers a closure or alignment relation that is not the symmetry group defined in Section 4.1. For general partially observed sets, pairwise differences need not form a subgroup and their generated closure can greatly overestimate the actual invariance structure.

The mathematical treatment of Lie-group geometry is incomplete. Connectedness does not ensure a globally well-defined logarithm, including on compact groups such as SO(3), where the logarithm is multivalued and discontinuous at π rotations. The GL(2)+ matrix-composition prior can also produce elements for which a real matrix logarithm is unavailable or ambiguous. The paper does not specify branch choices, failure handling, or numerical consequences, despite Algorithm 1 requiring log(g^{-1}). The claimed Riemannian loss is likewise not concretely specified for each group.

The evidence for “last-minute mode convergence” is technically questionable. Appendix D computes a purported conditional likelihood by inverting an interpolant and then integrating the learned marginal velocity field. The marginal flow does not provide the conditional density p(x_t|x_1) in this manner; for the stated deterministic interpolation, that density instead follows directly from the source distribution and a change of variables. Periodic boundary handling on SO(2) is also unclear. Consequently, the posterior entropy plots do not convincingly validate the proposed explanation, even if the time-reweighting heuristic empirically helps.

The evaluation is too narrow for the broad claims. All datasets, including the “real-world” ModelNet10 experiment, are artificially generated by applying known target groups to canonical objects. There is no evaluation on naturally occurring unknown symmetries, unseen shapes, approximate symmetries, noisy observations despite mentioning them, or downstream equivariant learning. The ModelNet experiment uses only 100 selected objects and does not report a train/test generalization protocol.

The baseline study is inadequate. Only LieGAN is compared, despite discussion of several relevant recent approaches. The paper acknowledges that LieGAN requires a suitable multimodal prior for discrete groups but compares against configurations seemingly tailored to continuous symmetries, making the large discrete-group advantage difficult to interpret. No comparison is made with finite-group or canonicalization-based discovery methods.

Reproducibility and statistical support are weak. Results are single numbers without multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, dataset sizes for the generated training sets, training epochs, stopping criteria, inference step counts, or sufficiently precise definitions of the group metric and empirical Wasserstein computation. No code or artifact is provided. Some implementation details are present, but not enough to reproduce or assess robustness.

Presentation is generally clear, but several statements overreach the evidence: the method is said to cover approximate symmetries without a corresponding formulation or experiment; ModelNet results are characterized as discovery on real-world data despite synthetic group augmentation; and improved downstream sample efficiency and generalization are suggested without downstream evaluation. These issues, together with the unsupported central identification claim, outweigh the promising formulation and warrant rejection rather than a borderline score.

strengths: Originality: Reframing symmetry discovery as distribution learning over a hypothesis Lie group is a creative and appealing perspective. The same construction handles continuous and discrete candidates without requiring a hand-specified generator basis or coefficient distribution.

Soundness: The experiments consistently show sharply concentrated transformations near the intended C4, tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral, and SO(2) subgroups. The large gains over LieGAN on discrete groups are compelling within the tested protocol; for example, Table 2a reports 0.0885 versus 2.326 for the tetrahedral group and 0.118 versus 1.861 for the icosahedral group with the power schedule.

Analysis: The identification of last-minute mode convergence is insightful. The posterior-entropy and trajectory analyses provide a useful empirical explanation, while the time-sampling ablation demonstrates that the proposed power schedule materially improves the difficult icosahedral case.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and visually effective. Algorithms 1–3 make the training and group-element generation procedures easy to follow, and the appendix provides useful implementation and diagnostic material.

Significance: A unified approach to discovering discrete and continuous symmetries could be valuable for geometric learning. The results across SO(2), GL(2)+, and SO(3), including partial observations and point masking, establish a promising proof of concept.

Limitations and ethics: The paper honestly acknowledges its limited scale, sensitivity to the hypothesis-group parameterization, and challenges for non-compact or high-dimensional groups. No material ethical concern is apparent, and the disclosed LLM usage is appropriately transparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central assertion that the learned distribution has support equal to the true subgroup is not established theoretically. In fact, a regular finite-time ODE flow cannot map a full-dimensional continuous prior exactly onto a lower-dimensional continuous subgroup or a finite set of atoms while remaining an invertible flow. The observed peaks are therefore approximate concentration, not literal support recovery. The endpoint singularity implicated by last-minute convergence makes this distinction central rather than merely terminological.

The explanation that non-symmetry transformations produce inconsistent directions that cancel while true symmetries yield a coherent field is heuristic. No identifiability or recovery result specifies when the generated Mg distribution equals H, excludes spurious transformations, or remains valid with multiple orbits, nontrivial stabilizers, nonuniform data, finite samples, or approximate symmetries.

The derivation explicitly obtains a unique Lie-algebra coordinate only when the data stabilizer is trivial, but this assumption is not included clearly in the main formulation or reconciled with ModelNet objects that may possess intrinsic symmetries. Global logarithms are also multivalued or discontinuous on groups such as SO(3), despite the paper suggesting that connectedness gives a well-defined logarithm.

Evaluation breadth is limited. The only quantitative baseline is LieGAN, whose fixed coefficient prior is acknowledged to be poorly suited to discrete groups; discrete-symmetry methods and the closely related generative/canonicalization approach discussed in related work are not compared. Consequently, the very large discrete-group advantage does not yet establish state-of-the-art symmetry discovery broadly.

The purported real-world evaluation uses ModelNet10 shapes that the authors synthetically rotate by known groups. It demonstrates recovery under more complex observations, but not discovery of naturally occurring, unknown, approximate, or object-dependent symmetries. The partial-C4 experiment similarly recovers the closure of pairwise relative transformations even though the observed distribution is not globally C4-invariant, so its interpretation as symmetry recovery needs greater precision.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper does not report random-seed variation or uncertainty, dataset sizes for the generated transformations, training epochs and stopping rules, inference step counts used for quantitative results, full LieGAN tuning details, or sufficiently precise metric conventions for every group. No code or artifact availability statement is provided. Single-run point estimates are especially concerning for adversarial and flow-based comparisons.

The power-schedule parameter is selected and evaluated on the same SO(3)-to-Ico setting, and its claim of working across discrete groups lacks broader controlled ablations. Robustness is tested only with mild 5–10% point masking; there is no study of observation noise, unequal group-element frequencies, approximate symmetries, hypothesis-group misspecification, or scalability.

Overall, the paper contains a strong idea and encouraging evidence, but the unsupported support-recovery interpretation, narrow and potentially favorable baseline comparison, synthetic nature of the evaluation, and incomplete reproducibility prevent reliable acceptance in its current form. A revised paper that formalizes approximate concentration, broadens comparisons, and reports statistically robust experiments could become a strong contribution.

strengths: Originality/significance: LieFlow offers an interesting formulation of symmetry discovery as learning a transformation distribution on a hypothesis Lie group. A single framework handles continuous, discrete, and conditional/partial symmetries, and the analysis of “last-minute convergence” motivates a simple, useful power time schedule.

Empirical evidence is broad for a methods paper: experiments cover SO(2), GL(2)+, SO(3), several finite rotation groups, two continuous subgroups, partial symmetries, noise, ModelNet10, and MI-Motion. On transformed ModelNet10, LieFlow substantially improves W1 over LieGAN, SGM, and Augerino for Tet, Oct, and Ico, while remaining competitive for SO(2).

The use of geodesic Wasserstein distance and improvement relative to random sampling is more informative than relying only on qualitative transformation plots. Results include three-seed variability, a noise study, a schedule ablation, and a runtime comparison.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. Algorithms specify training and sampling, appendices explain the induced vector field and stabilizer issue, and the limitations section candidly discusses hypothesis-group selection, continuous stabilizers, logarithm ambiguities, scalability, and the absence of an explicit algebraic presentation.

The research-ethics treatment is appropriate for the low-risk setting: the paper warns that incorrectly inferred symmetries can create misleading inductive biases or scientific conclusions and discloses LLM use.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central theoretical claim is not established. The paper repeatedly says that the learned distribution’s support “reveals” or “corresponds to” H, but Theorem B.4 proves only supp(p_theta) subseteq H, not H subseteq supp(p_theta). A sampler supported only on the identity would satisfy this conclusion without discovering H. No coverage, non-collapse, or recovery-rate result rules this out.

The theorem relies on very strong assumptions that largely encode the desired conclusion. In particular, Assumption B.1 assumes ideal convergence and support consistency, while B.2 assumes (Gx) intersect S = Hx for every observed point. These conditions fail for partial/approximate symmetries—the settings highlighted as contributions—and the paper gives no corresponding guarantees there. Matching the generated marginal data distribution also does not generally identify global symmetries because sample-dependent transformations can transport points within the support without preserving the full distribution.

The explanation that nonsymmetry targets “cancel out” while symmetry targets form a coherent field is intuitive but unproved and is not isolated empirically. The actual conditional-flow optimum can select sample-dependent transports, and the manuscript does not characterize when all elements of H, with the intended weights, must emerge.

The discrete-group comparison to LieGAN is not fully convincing. The paper notes that LieGAN requires a multimodal/delta-mixture coefficient prior for discrete groups, yet evaluates it with a uniform coefficient distribution that is structurally poorly matched to a finite target. Thus, the largest reported gains partly compare against a deliberately unsuitable configuration. Baseline hyperparameter searches and matched tuning budgets are not documented.

Most quantitative benchmarks are constructed by applying the target group to one tetrahedron or 100 selected ModelNet shapes, so the ground-truth structure is unusually clean and the same canonical objects appear throughout. There is no stated held-out-canonical evaluation. MI-Motion is the only unmodified real-data example, but its C4 interpretation is based on presumed axis-aligned preprocessing and is supported only qualitatively, without a statistical test, independent ground truth, or comparison beyond LieGAN.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the appendix omits important quantities such as training epochs/stopping rules, batch sizes for most experiments, synthetic dataset sizes, ODE solver and inference-step settings, baseline-specific optimization details, checkpoint/model-selection rules, and compute for the full suite. No code or artifact availability statement is provided despite substantial implementation complexity.

Significance is limited by the absence of any downstream test showing that discovered symmetries improve an equivariant model or scientific analysis. The method also requires a hand-chosen, relatively low-dimensional hypothesis group and does not output generators or an algebraic group description, making “discovery” dependent on visual or sample-based support interpretation.

There are smaller technical/presentation issues: connectedness alone does not ensure a globally well-defined logarithm, density invariance is sometimes written as q(hx)=q(x) without accounting for pushforward/Jacobian effects for non-volume-preserving actions such as GL(2)+, and the three-seed evaluation is too small to substantiate broad state-of-the-art claims. Overall, the promising empirical idea merits further work, but the recovery claim, comparative evidence, and reproducibility need substantial strengthening before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Originality/significance: Recasting symmetry discovery as conditional flow matching over a hypothesis Lie group is an interesting perspective, and the framework targets continuous, discrete, and partially observed symmetries within one method.

Empirical promise: On controlled C4, tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral, and SO(2) benchmarks, LieFlow usually achieves substantially lower Wasserstein-1 error than LieGAN; the ModelNet10 comparisons additionally include SGM and Augerino and report three-seed variability.

The analysis of late convergence for discrete targets is useful. The power time schedule is simple, and the SO(3)-to-Ico ablation shows a clear improvement from 0.470 under uniform sampling to 0.104 at skewness 5.

Presentation is generally organized, with algorithms, derivations, extensive visualizations, a noise study, computational timing, and an unusually candid limitations section covering hypothesis-group selection, stabilizers, logarithm branches, scaling, and the lack of an explicit algebraic group presentation.

The impact statement appropriately warns that incorrectly inferred symmetries can induce misleading scientific conclusions or harmful downstream inductive biases. LLM use is disclosed, and I see no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central support-recovery result is much weaker than the paper's discovery claim. Theorem B.4 establishes only supp(p_theta) subseteq H, not equality or coverage of H; an identity-only sampler satisfies this conclusion. It therefore does not prove that Algorithm 3 recovers the symmetry group, its support, or even every connected/discrete component.

The theory assumes its most important property rather than deriving it: Assumption B.1 posits ideal optimization and that the generated marginal exactly equals q. Assumptions B.2 and B.3 further require every supported point in a G-orbit to arise from the same global H and every point stabilizer to lie in H. These strong conditions exclude many heterogeneous, partial, approximate, and continuously stabilized settings emphasized as motivations.

There is a noncommutative convention inconsistency. Equation 4 and the algorithms use x_t=exp(tA)x_0=exp(tA)g x_1, whereas Appendix A derives the group curve g_t=g exp(tA) and describes its induced path as g_t x_1. These coincide for SO(2) but generally not for SO(3) or GL(2). Consequently, the stated left-trivialized target-field derivation does not clearly justify the implemented interpolation and update in the main noncommutative experiments.

The explanation that nonsymmetries yield inconsistent directions that cancel while symmetries remain coherent is intuitive but unproved. A conditional flow can transport the randomly transformed marginal back to q through many couplings; marginal distribution matching alone does not identify a unique transformation distribution or guarantee group closure.

The purported real-world validation is not convincing. MI-Motion has no ground-truth symmetry, no quantitative metric, and no comparison beyond LieGAN. Moreover, Figure 6 is dominated by a very large identity-angle spike and does not visibly substantiate the textual claim of clear peaks at 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees. This could reflect identity collapse rather than reliable C4 discovery.

Most evidence is constructed using known target groups: a single arrow, one irregular tetrahedron, or ModelNet objects explicitly augmented by ground-truth transformations. There is no held-out symmetry test, downstream equivariant-learning evaluation, or measurement of invariance, group closure, precision/recall of recovered elements, or recovery under mixed orbit structures. Wasserstein distance to the construction transformations alone gives a narrow assessment.

Baseline coverage and tuning are insufficient for a state-of-the-art claim. Recent finite-group and generator-discovery methods discussed in related work are not evaluated, and only LieGAN is used on the synthetic benchmarks. The power-schedule skewness is selected directly using ground-truth Wasserstein error on the Ico setting, without a validation protocol or sensitivity analysis beyond that same target.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript gives architectures and some optimizer settings but omits essential details such as training epochs/stopping criteria, dataset sizes for most synthetic/ModelNet experiments, inference solver settings used for reported tables, complete MI-Motion preprocessing and training hyperparameters, and a code or configuration release. LLM-generated portions of model and visualization code make artifact availability particularly important.

Presentation overstates the contribution as learning directly in group space and recovering H. The network is conditioned on data-space points and emits algebra coordinates, while the only theorem proves exclusion of transformations outside H under restrictive assumptions. The manuscript should distinguish distribution preservation, subgroup containment, and full group identification.

Overall, the idea and controlled results are promising, but the theoretical gap, noncommutative derivation inconsistency, weak real-data evidence, and incomplete reproducibility leave the central symmetry-recovery claims insufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: Originality and significance: LieFlow offers a compelling reframing of symmetry discovery as learning a distribution over a hypothesis Lie group. Modeling the support of transformations provides a unified treatment of continuous, finite, and partially observed symmetries, unlike generator-based approaches that require a prescribed coefficient distribution.

Soundness and evidence: The controlled experiments cover C4, several finite SO(3) subgroups, continuous SO(2) subgroups, two hypothesis groups, partial symmetries, and noisy observations. Results over three seeds are consistently strong: for example, on ModelNet10 LieFlow obtains W1 values of 0.149, 0.097, and 0.129 for Tet, Oct, and Ico, respectively, substantially outperforming all reported baselines.

The identification and empirical analysis of last-minute mode convergence is insightful. The power time schedule is simple but effective, with the SO(3)-to-Ico ablation improving W1 from 0.470 under uniform sampling to 0.104 at skewness 5.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized, with intuitive trajectory and group-element visualizations, explicit training and sampling algorithms, a useful relative-to-random metric, runtime information, and a substantial appendix.

The limitations and impact discussions are unusually candid. They appropriately identify dependence on the hypothesis group, stabilizer and logarithm-map issues, lack of an explicit algebraic presentation, and the risk of interpreting approximate or biased symmetries as exact. No unresolved material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantee is materially weaker than the paper's central recovery language. Theorem B.4 proves only that the learned support is contained in H, not that it equals or covers H; a distribution concentrated on a proper subset, including potentially the identity, satisfies the conclusion. Moreover, the theorem assumes ideal convergence, globally generated support, and that every point stabilizer is already a global symmetry. These strong assumptions exclude important ambiguity, local-symmetry, and approximate-symmetry cases.

Most quantitative evidence is based on synthetically imposed transformations. ModelNet10 uses only 100 selected canonical shapes and is rotated using the known target group, so it remains a controlled synthetic-orbit benchmark rather than evidence of discovering naturally occurring object symmetries. MI-Motion is the only unmodified real-data example, and its C4 conclusion is qualitative and partly anticipated from axis-aligned preprocessing; there is no quantitative preservation test or downstream evaluation.

The GL(2)+ treatment needs clarification. Algorithm 1 requires log(g^-1), yet the matrix-composition prior can produce elements of GL+(2) that need not lie in the image of the real matrix exponential. Filtering only by determinant does not ensure that a real logarithm exists. The manuscript does not specify how invalid, complex, or numerically unstable logarithms are handled.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are not fully convincing. LieGAN is evaluated with a uniform coefficient prior even though the paper acknowledges that a multimodal discrete prior is the relevant configuration for finite groups. SGM and Augerino implementation and tuning details are sparse. Important information such as training duration, batch sizes for most experiments, integration-step choices, checkpoint selection, and code availability is also missing.

The evaluation establishes recovery accuracy but not the practical utility claimed in the motivation: no experiment uses the discovered transformations in an equivariant model, data augmentation pipeline, or scientific inference task. The selected power-schedule parameter is also tuned and evaluated on the same SO(3)-to-Ico setting, so evidence that it transfers without target-specific selection is limited.
